$comment: CANONICAL DESIGN TOKENS — single source of truth for the entire desktop.
Nothing downstream hardcodes a colour, spacing value, duration or easing curve.
Edit this file, then run `design/build-tokens.py` to regenerate every consumer:
quickshell/gelo/Theme/Tokens.qml         (Quickshell shell — bar/launcher/notifications)
sddm/themes/gelo-liquid/Theme/Tokens.qml (SDDM login theme — separate QML import root)
design/tokens.css                        (GTK / Waybar fallback tier)
hypr/tokens.conf                         (hyprland.conf + hyprlock.conf, hyprlang syntax)
All four generated files carry a do-not-edit header and are checked in, so a fresh
clone works without running the generator.
PS3 XMB, light/silver variant. Cold blues and silver over a near-white
surface, navy ink, one saturated blue accent. Still zero warm hues.
This is an INVERSION of the earlier dark palette, so two extra semantic
tokens exist that a dark theme did not need:
shade      — the dark colour shadows and scrims are built from. On a
light theme this can no longer be bg-0, which is now the
lightest surface; using it would make shadows invisible.
accent-ink — what sits ON the accent (the workspace blob). Previously
that was bg-0; on a light theme it has to be white.
NOT named on-accent: that camel-cases to `onAccent`, which
QML parses as a signal handler for a signal named
`accent`, and the whole singleton fails to load.
The field-* group is the wave shader's own ramp, kept separate from the
UI surfaces so the wallpaper can be more saturated than the chrome
sitting on top of it.
Accent still appears in EXACTLY three places: active workspace
indicator, focused window border, cursor.
The dark surface ramp, for GTK / libadwaita apps.
The shell chrome is light and the content windows are dark, which is the
same figure/ground call the terminal already makes: a file manager is a
window you look *into*, and the bar is a surface you look *at*. Two
families, one hue.
Anchored on terminal.background so the terminal and the file manager are
the same dark, not two darks that nearly match. bg-1 is terminal.ansi[0]
for the same reason.
accent is the LIGHT step here, not color.accent: #3478c4 is tuned to sit
on a near-white surface and falls below AA as link text on #14293f. Every
pair in this block is measured by `build-tokens.py --audit`.
Ghostty. A DARK terminal on a light desktop: strong figure/ground, and
light-on-dark text survives translucency far better than dark-on-light,
because whatever bleeds through a light desktop can only lighten the
background and dark-on-light loses contrast as it does.
The hue stays in the cold blue family so it still reads as part of the
wave field rather than a black hole punched in it.
TRADE-OFF, measured rather than assumed: transparency and contrast pull
against each other here. Every point of opacity given up lets more of a
bright field through, which lifts the effective background and shrinks
the ratio against the text. `opacity` is set where the measured contrast
still clears WCAG AA comfortably; see docs/CHANGES.md for the numbers.
HONEST DEVIATION: the rest of the system bans warm hues outright. A
terminal cannot honour that. ANSI 1/3/9/11 are load-bearing semantics —
git diff red, build warnings, test failures — and remapping them to blues
would break every tool that assumes them. They are kept desaturated and
cool-leaning so they sit in the palette rather than shouting out of it,
but they are genuinely red/yellow and that is deliberate.
opacity/blur are consumed by ghostty; the blur itself is done by
Hyprland, which only blurs windows that are actually translucent.
OFF by default and deliberately so: enabling it sends a request to a
third-party server (wttr.in) every 15 minutes, and with no location set
that server geolocates you by IP. Setting an explicit city is both
coarser and more reliable than IP geolocation.
Set enabled=true and location='Boston' (or similar) to turn it on.
How the system writes times and measurements. Here rather than at each
call site because four surfaces show a clock — bar, lock screen, SDDM
greeter, agenda — and a desktop that says 3:45 PM in one place and 15:45
in another is the same failure as two shades of the same blue.
units: 'imperial' (°F, inches) or 'metric' (°C, mm).

space.$comment: 4px base grid. Every gap, padding and margin in every component snaps to this scale.

radius.$comment: Snapped to the 4px grid. `full` is the pill/blob terminal value.

$comment: One geometric/thin display sans everywhere — the XMB look is a single
voice, not a mono/sans split.
Michroma or Eurostile would be the real thing; neither is installed nor
packaged for Arch, so this is the plan's sanctioned fallback: a system
sans at light weight. Inter Display ships Thin/ExtraLight/Light and is
the most geometric face available here.
Numerals in the clock and commit hash use tabular figures (tnum) so they
do not jitter — that is what mono was previously buying us.
$displayComment: Geist (Vercel, OFL) — clean geometric grotesque, holds up at 11px.
Michroma was tried first as the literal XMB face and was too mannered
for a bar that is read constantly rather than looked at.
Geist is a variable font with a real weight axis, so unlike Michroma the
300/400 weight tokens do apply. QML's font value type exposes `family`
but not `families`, so per-glyph fallback is fontconfig's job; the list
here is consumed by the CSS tier.
Alternatives already installed if you want to switch (one token edit):
Figtree, Inter Display, Nimbus Sans (Helvetica clone).

weight.$comment: 300 default (thin), 400 for emphasis. NEVER 500+ — weight is not how this system creates hierarchy; glow and opacity are.

type.$trackingComment: +0.02em on labels. Open tracking is a core part of the XMB feel. QML letterSpacing is in pixels, so this is a ratio applied against pixelSize via Tokens.tracking().

motion.$comment: Slightly softer landing than the previous expo-out. --dur-slow is specifically the ripple propagation time.

$comment: Chrome / reflection — the PS3 XMB material language. This REPLACES the
previous frosted-glass approach entirely: no backdrop blur anywhere, and
the compositor layerrules that produced it are gone.
Four rules, applied identically everywhere:
1. Brushed metal. Raised surfaces carry a subtle vertical gradient,
`bg-1` at the top fading a few percent darker at the bottom. Enough
to read as material; not enough to read as a gradient.
2. Selection is GLOW, not outline and not fill. Nothing gets boxed when
selected — it blooms. This is the single most identifiable XMB trait.
3. Reflection beneath elements: a flipped, heavily faded, gradient-masked
copy. The 'icons floating over water' effect.
4. Motion lives in the wave field BEHIND the UI, not in the UI. Elements
do not deform. Interactions emit a ripple that propagates outward
through the background shader from the point of interaction.
Bloom radiating outward. `extent` is how far the halo reaches in
PIXELS, not a scale factor.
It used to be a multiplier (spread: 1.7), which meant the halo grew
with whatever it surrounded: fine on a 20px icon, but a 320px-wide
password field got a 112px halo and read as a blue fog around the
control. Light spreads a roughly fixed distance from a source; it does
not get bigger because the source is wider.

reflection.$comment: heightRatio is the fraction of the source height that gets mirrored before the mask fades it out.

blob.$comment: The travelling workspace indicator. Kept deliberately: its two edges animate at different durations so it stretches across the gap and settles, rather than sliding. `squash` is the vertical compression while in motion, which conserves apparent volume.

$comment: The top bar, which is three separate panels rather than one strip:
workspaces on the left, clock and window title centred, status on the
right. Each is its own layer surface with its own chrome, so the gaps
between them show the wave field rather than more chrome.
height is the panel height. 48 rather than 36 because the workspace
numbers carry reflections beneath them and those need somewhere to land.
Only ONE of the three may hold an exclusive zone. Layer-shell exclusive
zones on the same edge SUM, so three panels each reserving 48px would
push windows down by 144.
radius is larger than material.chrome.radius: at 8px a 48px-tall panel
reads as a strip that has been cut off, and these are now free-standing
objects with the wallpaper visible on both sides of them.
The now-playing readout scrolls: the text enters from the right edge,
travels left until it has fully left, then re-enters from the right.
This is a deliberate exception to the rule that motion lives in the wave
field rather than in the interface (design.md 5). A track title is the
one label here that is routinely longer than the space it has, and the
alternative was an ellipsis that hides the artist forever.
speed is px/second and is what keeps it honest — duration is derived
from it, so a long title takes longer rather than scrolling faster. A
fixed duration would make every title move at a different speed, which
reads as the interface being unsure of itself.
width is fixed, not fitted to the text: a viewport that resized per
track would move the workspace indicator next to it on every song.
The panel that drops out of the bar when you click the now-playing
readout. Album art, title/artist/album, a seekable progress track, and
previous / play / next / shuffle.
There is no queue, and it is not an oversight. MPRIS exposes a queue only
through the optional org.mpris.MediaPlayer2.TrackList interface, Spotify
reports HasTrackList = false and does not implement it, and Quickshell's
Mpris module has no TrackList binding to read it with even where a player
does. Spotify's real queue is Web-API-only and needs OAuth.
artSize is square. A non-square cover is letterboxed rather than
cropped: album art is the one image in this system that is somebody
else's composition.
The auto-hiding dock at the bottom edge.
revealStrip is the always-live band of screen the pointer has to touch
to bring it up. It is the only part of the dock that is permanently
interactive, so it is the whole cost of the feature: too thin and the
dock is unreachable, too thick and it fires while you reach for a
window edge. 6px is roughly one flick of overshoot.
hideDelay stops the dock flickering out the moment the pointer crosses
a gap between two icons.
iconRest/iconHover are the icon box before and after magnification.
Growing the box rather than scaling the image keeps the icon on the
pixel grid, which matters at this size — logos go mushy when scaled to
a fractional width.
radius is the plate's own corner, deliberately larger than
material.chrome.radius: every other surface is anchored to a screen
edge, and this one floats free.

ripple.$comment: Propagation through the background field, in normalised screen units per second. maxConcurrent bounds the uniform array the wallpaper shader reads.
